Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery. Physical affection such as hugs is difficult to connect to robbery-related threat activation without any supporting appraisal, memory, or strategy content, and it conflicts with the otherwise stranger/sudden-movement threat profile. Crash imagery is more characteristic of road traffic trauma than robbery and lacks any plausible link to the reported threat items.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger item about cars being hit in an accident is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of mugging/robbery. The other trigger and threat items coherently suggest interpersonal danger and hypervigilance around strangers/crowding, but crash imagery points to a motor vehicle trauma theme that is not reflected elsewhere in the profile or in the cognitive formulation. This is more than unusual; it appears to reference a different trauma context.

vignette: Ramesh had always been a man who felt safe in his own skin. As an electrician, he was used to working with his hands and being around people, whether it was fixing a faulty wiring in a crowded office building or installing new lights in a residential neighborhood. But all of that changed one fateful evening six months ago, when he was mugged by two strangers on his way home from work. Ramesh remembered the smell of alcohol on their breath as they pushed him against the wall and demanded his wallet. The sudden movement had startled him, and for a moment, he was frozen in fear. One of them had grabbed his arm, twisting it behind his back, while the other rummaged through his pockets. Ramesh recalled feeling helpless, unable to move or defend himself. After that night, Ramesh began to notice changes in himself. He would wake up from nightmares, his heart racing, with vivid images of those two strangers still etched in his mind. The dream residue lingered throughout the day, making him feel on edge and anxious. Simple tasks like grocery shopping became daunting ordeals as he found himself scanning crowded places for potential threats. One evening, while out with his wife, Ramesh caught a whiff of alcohol at a nearby restaurant. Instantly, he was transported back to that night, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. He quickly excused himself and stepped outside, citing a need for fresh air. His wife, concerned about his well-being, asked if everything was alright. Ramesh brushed it off, not wanting to worry her. As time went on, Ramesh's hypervigilance grew more pronounced. At night, he would lie awake, listening for any unusual sounds outside their home. He became increasingly paranoid about strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations like walking down the street or chatting with a neighbor. His wife noticed that he was becoming withdrawn and isolated, avoiding social gatherings and family events. Ramesh couldn't shake off the feeling of vulnerability. Sudden movements by others would put him immediately on guard - a coworker's sudden laughter, a child's playful shout, or even his own wife's unexpected touch. He began to question whether he was overreacting, but deep down, he knew that these responses were rooted in something real. At work, Ramesh found it increasingly difficult to focus. His clients would often remark on the smell of alcohol from a nearby bar or restaurant, sending Ramesh into a tailspin of anxiety. He started avoiding jobs that required him to work late at night or in crowded areas. His business began to suffer as he turned down more and more projects. Ramesh's wife grew concerned about his well-being and encouraged him to seek help. What finally brought him to therapy was the realization that he couldn't continue living like this - constantly on edge, avoiding the things he loved, and pushing away those closest to him. As he sat in the therapist's office, Ramesh expressed a deep-seated fear: "What if I'm never able to feel safe again?"
